s0_title: S7900 odd-form insertion with lead clinching for 5 SPD boards
s0_subtitle: One 6-head S7900 with a 15-layer tray feeder and customised grippers inserts two bulky SPD modules and clinches every lead before wave soldering.
s1_title: From conveyor to clinched, solder-ready board
s1_steps0b: Inlet conveyor brings the board or fixture into the S7900; board in and out takes 4 s, mark recognition 1 s.
s1_steps1b: Six heads with customised grippers pick SPD modules from a 15-layer tray feeder: 0.3 s pick, 0.3 s insert per part.
s1_steps2b: Each lead is bent 15–30° under the board right after insertion, 1.5 s per part, so parts cannot float in the wave.
s1_steps3b: Outlet conveyor passes the board to wave soldering through a SMEMA interface.
s2_title: Five boards, two bulky SPD modules
s2_note: PCB sizes given: Board 1 233 × 139 mm, Board 3 382 × 330 mm (panel). Others to be confirmed.
s3_title: 30 – 59 boards an hour with every lead clinched
s3_note: Cycle = rounds × (6 × 0.3 s pick + 1.8 s head move + 6 × 0.3 s insert) + 1.5 s clinch per part + 4 s board in/out + 1 s marks. Board 4 without clinch: 3,600 ÷ 32 s gives 112, the proposal states 105; to be confirmed.
s4_title: Up to 79 % more boards an hour than the current benchmark
s4_text: Without clinching, the S7900 runs Board 1 at 147 boards an hour against 82 and Board 3 at 96 against 63 on the reference machine. Configuration: 1 × S7900 6-head core machine, 1 × STF248E tray feeder, 6 × customised 24JD04L49 grippers.
s5_title: Why the tray feeder wins for bulky SPD modules
s5_note: Boards per refill: Board 1 90 vs 38.85, Board 2 94.5 vs 40.8, Board 3 70 vs 29, Board 4 84 vs 35, Board 5 52 vs 22 (theoretical).
s6_title: Clinched leads keep SPD modules flat through the wave
s6_caption: Lead clinching unit and bend patterns
s6_b0: Automatic lead bending of about 15–30° right after insertion.
s6_b1: Clinch length 1.3–1.8 mm under the board.
s6_b2: Outward bend, inner bend, circular and 2-turn patterns.
s6_b3: Stops component floating during wave soldering and keeps modules vertical.
s6_b4: Adds 1.5 s per part to the cycle, shown in the clinch columns.
s7_note: One slide of the proposal lists a 4-head version at 1100 × 1500 × 1700 mm; the 6-head version is used here.

s8_title: Feeding and handling around the S7900
s8_caption: Tray feeder magazine loaded with trays
s8_b0: Customised balanced tray feeder: dual drive at 0.5–0.8 MPa, 2000 W, buttons and screen.
s8_b1: Handles SMDs, small passives and odd-shaped parts, with alarms and maintenance prompts.
s8_b3: Inlet and outlet conveyors: 900 ± 20 mm height, left to right by default, 75 kg.

s9_title: What the parts, boards and trays need
s9_caption: Tray packaging concept for the two modules
s9_b0: Leads 0.5 × 7 mm bend easily and cannot be modified: handle with the gripper and tray design.
s9_b1: Widen board holes from 1.2 × 10.2 mm to 2.4 × 10.2 mm for more insertion tolerance.
s9_b2: All pins in one orientation to avoid pick-up interference.
s9_b3: Tray: width 150–340 mm, depth 90–230 mm, height 5–36 mm, 500 g including parts.
s9_b4: ≥5 mm from divider top to part top; ≥5 mm gap in the gripper closing direction.
s9_b5: Part-to-grid gap within 0.5 mm, burr-free walls, long side across the tray.

ans_h2: How do you automate insertion of bulky SPD modules with clinched leads?
ans_p: Use one 6-head S7900 odd-form inserter with a 15-layer tray feeder, customised grippers and lead clinching. It inserts and clinches 20–48 SPD modules per board at 30–59 boards an hour, or 74–148 without clinching, with one tray load covering 52–94 boards.

blog_lead: Eight short reads built on this solution. Tap a title to open it.
faq_h2: Questions SPD makers ask about this solution
a1: Bulky SPD modules can lift in the wave. Bending each lead 15–30° right after insertion holds the module flat and vertical through soldering.
q2: How much does clinching slow the cycle?
a2: It adds 1.5 s per part. Output drops from 74–148 to 30–59 boards an hour across the five boards.
q3: Why a tray feeder instead of tubes?
a3: One 15-layer tray feeder holds 1,890–2,520 modules against 816–1,056 in six tube feeders, with pick rejection under 0.3 % instead of 0.5–2 %.
q4: How often must an operator refill?
a4: Theoretically every 52–94 boards with trays, against every 22–41 boards with tubes.
q5: Do our parts or boards need changes?
a5: Pins should all face one way, and widening holes from 1.2 × 10.2 to 2.4 × 10.2 mm adds tolerance. Trays follow the design rules in this page.
q6: What do you need to start?
a6: Sample modules, bare boards and fixtures. We design trays and grippers and run a sample to confirm cycle and output.
bl1t: Why SPD modules resist automatic insertion
bl1s: Bulky bodies, soft leads and wave soldering.
bl1p1: A 55.9 mm tall SPD module is the part most lines still insert by hand.
bl1p2: Its weight, height and soft leads make it tip, miss holes or lift in the wave.
bl1p3: Treat it as three problems: how it is presented, how it is gripped and how it is held after insertion.
bl1p4: The S7900 answers all three with a tray feeder, customised grippers and lead clinching, at 0.7 s per part and ±0.06 mm.
bl1p5: List every hand-inserted part on your boards and sort by size and weight before you plan.
bl1p6: Send us your heaviest part first; it sets the design.
bl2t: Clinching: the step that stops floating parts
bl2s: How a 15–30° bend saves the wave.
bl2p1: A module that floats in the wave becomes a rework job, or a field failure.
bl2p2: Fixtures alone cannot hold every module on a dense panel.
bl2p3: Bend the leads under the board right after insertion, before the board moves.
bl2p4: The S7900 clinch unit bends 1.3–1.8 mm of lead about 15–30°, outward, inward, circular or 2-turn, adding 1.5 s per part.
bl2p5: Check clinch angle on first boards of each shift.
bl2p6: Ask us for a clinch sample on your boards.
bl3t: Reading a cycle-time sheet in five minutes
bl3p1: Cycle sheets look complex; they are five numbers.
bl3p2: Without them, buyers compare brochure speeds that never match their boards.
bl3p3: Add rounds × (picks + head move + inserts), clinch per part, board in/out and marks.
bl3p4: With 0.3 s pick, 0.3 s insert, 1.8 s move, 1.5 s clinch, 4 s handling and 1 s marks, a 21-point board runs 24.8 s unclinched and 60.8 s clinched.
bl3p5: Re-run the sum when the BOM changes.
bl3p6: Send your BOM for a cycle sheet.
bl4t: Tray or tube for bulky parts
bl4p1: Tubes look cheap until you count the refills.
bl4p2: Six tube feeders still hold fewer parts than one tray magazine and jam more often.
bl4p3: Compare full load, boards per refill and rejection rate, not unit packaging cost alone.
bl4p4: One 15-layer tray feeder holds 1,890–2,520 modules against 816–1,056 in six tube feeders; rejection under 0.3 % against 0.5–2 %.
bl4p5: Track refills per shift after start-up.
bl4p6: Ask for the tray-versus-tube sheet for your parts.
bl5s: Seven rules from the feeder side.
bl5p1: Most pick errors start in the tray, not the machine.
bl5p2: Loose cavities, burrs and wrong orientation make grippers miss.
bl5p3: Fix the spacing, the clearances and the orientation before you order trays.
bl5p4: Keep trays 150–340 × 90–230 × 5–36 mm and 500 g, ≥5 mm clearances, part-to-grid gap within 0.5 mm, long side across the tray.
bl5p5: Inspect new tray batches for burrs and warp.
bl5p6: Send your part sample; we draw the tray.
bl6t: Small board changes that raise insertion yield
bl6p1: A millimetre on the board can save hours of rework.
bl6p2: Tight holes and mixed pin orientation cause stuck and missed inserts.
bl6p3: Give the lead room and keep every pin the same way.
bl6p4: Here, widening holes from 1.2 × 10.2 mm to 2.4 × 10.2 mm adds tolerance; 0.5 × 7 mm leads are kept as they are and handled by gripper design.
bl6p5: Add these checks to your DFM review.
bl6p6: Ask us to review your next layout.
bl7s: Why standard nozzles drop SPD modules.
bl7p1: Vacuum nozzles struggle with tall, heavy, uneven parts.
bl7p2: Dropped modules stop the machine and damage leads.
bl7p3: Design the gripper around the part body and the tray, then prove it on samples.
bl7p4: This cell uses six customised 24JD04L49 grippers on the S7900's six heads.
bl7p5: Keep spare gripper fingers and check wear monthly.
bl7p6: Send samples for a gripper design.

bl8p3: Ship samples, approve trays and grippers, then run your boards.
bl8p4: Southern Machinery includes installation and training, dispatches spare parts within 1 day and delivers custom tray solutions in 5 days.
bl8p5: Review output and rejects monthly after start-up.
